readerTitle: Your first customers should be the easiest to win, not the biggest
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (B2B 회계 서비스 회사, 소매 체인 안의 데이터 팀) · 첫 공략 집단 개념은 Moore(1991)의 비치헤드 논의를 참고
insight: 첫 고객은 가장 큰 시장이 아니라, 지금 가장 아프고, 닿기 쉽고, 서로 이야기하는 좁은 집단에서 고른다.
misconception: 처음부터 가장 넓은 시장이나 가장 큰 고객 하나를 노려야 빨리 큰다.

sources.text: Moore, G. A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness. (첫 공략 집단, 'beachhead' 개념)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 두 사업 사례와 숫자(점포 120곳, 지역 점포 8곳 등)는 모두 가상입니다. 실제 기업이나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
'beachhead'라는 표현과 노르망디 상륙 비유가 Moore의 Crossing the Chasm에서 쓰였다는 점을 게시 전에 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 비유만 짧게 적었습니다.

cards.title: Your first customers should be the easiest to win, not the biggest
body: Two launches, same month. A small bookkeeping firm offers a new service. A data team inside a retail chain releases a new tool to colleagues.
Both have something good. Both face the same first question, and most people answer it the wrong way: *who do we sell to first?*

image.label: Two doors: a small firm's office and a corporate team room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 작은 회계 사무소 문, 오른쪽은 큰 회사 안 팀 회의실 문. 두 문 앞에 각각 같은 질문 말풍선 "Who first?". 실제 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The bookkeeping firm picks its first customers.
body: Rhea runs a five-person bookkeeping firm. Her new service turns messy receipts into tax-ready books within a week. She has time and money to chase one group properly.
Who should she go after first?

options.text: Every small business in the city. It's the biggest market
options.feedback: The market is huge, but a bakery, a law office and a plumber need different things and never talk to each other. Her small budget gets spread thin.

options.text: Dental clinics in her region. Their books look alike and owners meet monthly
options.feedback: A smaller group, but they share the same pain, she can reach them in one room, and each happy clinic can tell the others.

options.text: One large hospital group. A single contract could fill her calendar
options.feedback: One big win would help cash flow. But the sale could take a year, and one customer's demands can reshape her whole service.

cards.title: Three quick tests for a first group.
body: The dental clinics passed all three tests. "All small businesses" passed none of them well.

breakdown.label: It hurts now
breakdown.detail: Clinics scramble every tax season with the same kinds of receipts

breakdown.label: You can reach them
breakdown.detail: One regional association, one monthly meeting

breakdown.label: They talk to each other
breakdown.detail: A clinic owner trusts another clinic owner's advice

cards.title: Your first segment
body: Your **first segment** is the narrow group you win before anyone else. Pick it by how fast you can win it, not by how big it is.
Geoffrey Moore called this a *beachhead*, after the small stretch of shore an army takes before moving inland. You win one group completely, then use it to reach the next.
A big market you can't win is worth less than a small one you can.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders often launch "for all teams" because the product can technically serve anyone. Picking one job title in one industry makes ads cheaper, onboarding simpler and reviews more convincing to the next buyer.

cards.title: Winning one group makes the next one cheaper.
body: When customers in a tight group talk, each sale makes the next one easier. The tenth dental clinic hears about Rhea from three others before she calls.
Spread across all small businesses, every sale starts from zero. No one has heard of her, and no one's story applies to the next customer.
A narrow group also teaches faster. Similar customers raise similar problems, so the service gets better for everyone at once.

cards.title: The first group is a door, not the whole house.
body: Once dentists are won, the next step is a group that looks similar: orthodontists, then vets, then physiotherapy clinics. Same type of books, same tax worries, overlapping networks.
Each new group is chosen with the same three tests, plus one more: **can my wins in the last group convince this one?**

image.label: Stepping stones from dentists to nearby groups
image.brief: 징검다리 일러스트. 첫 돌 "Dental clinics"가 가장 크고 색이 진함. 이어지는 돌에 "Orthodontists", "Vets", "Physio clinics". 돌 사이에 작은 말풍선으로 입소문을 표현.

cards.title: Narrow has to still be worth it.
body: A first group can be too small. If it can't pay enough to keep the business alive while you grow, it's a hobby, not a beachhead.
It also has to actually feel the pain. Friends, family or a friendly boss are easy to reach, but polite interest isn't the same as needing you.
And don't stay forever. A first segment that becomes your only segment can cap your growth.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a retail chain.
body: You lead a small data team at a chain of 120 stores. Your new tool suggests what to reorder each week, so shelves stay full. You need the tool to spread across the company.
Where do you start?

options.text: Launch to all 120 stores at once with a company-wide email
options.feedback: Maximum reach on day one, but most stores ignore it, the bugs hit everyone, and early complaints become the tool's reputation.

options.text: Start with 8 stores in one region whose manager complains about empty shelves and runs a weekly call with store leads
options.feedback: They feel the pain, you can reach them in one call, and their results travel to other regions. You trade speed for a story others will believe.

options.text: Start with head-office finance, since they control budgets
options.feedback: A powerful sponsor helps later. But finance doesn't restock shelves, so you get approval without real users or proof.

cards.title: Win a small group completely before chasing a big one.
body: Pick first customers who hurt now, are easy to reach, and talk to each other. Their wins become your best marketing for the next group.
**Try it today:** list three groups you could sell to. Score each on pain, reach and how much they talk to each other. Which one wins?
